extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners of literature and the visual arts (particularly painters and essayists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for selecting and composing subjects for history painting (and relatedly for using imagery and moral example in essays): choosing moments that can be represented instantaneously, that yield distinct attitudes and varied passions, and that provide instructive variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be instantaneous
rubrics_metrics.description: He must have an action not successive but instantaneous; for the time of a picture is a single moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A picture represents a single moment — subjects that require a sequence of events (e.g., the many successive deeds in the death of Hercules) fail because their essence cannot be united in one instant. Anti‑pattern: choosing a subject whose emotional or narrative impact depends on showing a series of actions rather than one decisive moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be circumstantial and distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must be circumstantial and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pictorial subject should include a clear, observable circumstance or gesture that conveys the incident without recourse to words. Example of failure: a supplication scene from Homer where language supplies what no pictorial peculiarity can, so the sentiment cannot be effectively conveyed in paint alone. Scoring note: if viewers require explanatory text to understand the scene, the subject is poorly chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject must excite varied passions among actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The event painted must be such as excites passion, and different passions in the several actors, or a tumult of contending passions in the chief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects that permit contrasting emotional responses across figures (surprise mingled with joy, prudence clouded by solicitude, composure in the dying hero, etc.). Examples of good subjects: the discovery of Ulysses by his nurse (surprise + joy + prudence), the death of Epaminondas (mixture of gladness and grief, attendants' varied passions). Anti‑pattern: emotionally monotonous scenes with only one affective tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition should allow variety and clear roles for figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The picture, having only two figures, will want variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For richness and instructive power, compositions often benefit from multiple figures showing diverse reactions and roles; a single pair may lack narrative and emotional scope. Example: prefer scenes with attendants, messengers, and principal character to create contrasts. Note: too many unrelated details can diffuse the focus — variety must serve unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose historical subjects that can be unified in a single moment and yield instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not very easy to find an action or event that can be efficaciously represented by a painter... If some proper disposition could be contrived, [the dissolution of the parliament by Cromwell] would make a picture of unexampled variety, and irresistible instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick historical moments that combine a decisive instant with morally or politically instructive content. Guidance includes imagining the precise point to depict (e.g., Cromwell ordering the bauble removed) where faces and gestures supply the lesson. Anti‑pattern: grand episodes without a single telling instant or without instructive contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrait painting's social/aesthetic function
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrait painting is employed in diffusing friendship, in reviving tenderness, in quickening the affections of the absent, and continuing the presence of the dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the value of portraiture beyond mere likeness: its purpose can be social, mnemonic, and affective. Caution against undervaluing portrait work or diverting portrait artists exclusively to historical or 'sublime' subjects at the expense of this social function. Example: Reynolds should not abandon portraiture for airy fiction if it neglects friendship's uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural imagery to admonish and awaken action
rubrics_metrics.description: All the appearances of nature uniformly conspire... The day has been considered as an image of the year, and the year as the representation of life. The morning answers to the spring... the night with its silence and darkness shows the winter... the night cometh when no man can work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral or didactic writing, employ cycles and phenomena of nature (day/night, seasons, sun/moon) as vivid metaphors to remind readers of time's passage and motivate timely action. Example usage: exhorting readers to give while recipients can enjoy it, or to avoid procrastination. Anti‑pattern: abstract exhortation without concrete natural imagery to fix attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure recollection into collection and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory has two offices: collection and distribution; by one images are accumulated, and by the other produced for use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating memory in essays or narrative, consider the developmental phases: early life as a time of collection (gathering impressions) and later life as distribution (displaying and using accumulated knowledge). Use this framework to structure memoiristic material or to explain shifts in a character's relationship to knowledge. Example: older characters as dispensers of accumulated stores; younger characters as avid collectors. Antipattern: treating memory as a static faculty without functional stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolation writing: prefer religious hope over abstract stoicism
rubrics_metrics.description: Real alleviation of the loss of friends, and rational tranquillity, in the prospect of our own dissolution, can be received only from the promises of Him in whose hands are life and death... Philosophy may infuse stubbornness, but Religion only can give patience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In writings addressing grief, the essay recommends grounding consolation in religious hope and promises of an afterlife rather than solely in philosophical stoicism or Epicurean resignation. Use scripture‑rooted assurances to offer 'rational tranquillity.' Anti‑pattern: offering only abstract philosophical maxims that may silence but not truly comfort the bereaved.
